c.st: Re: C as used/implemented in practice
c.x:
The point here is not particularly about signedness, it's that UB allows better optimizations to be performed.

If overflow is defined to wrap around then it's potentially an infinite loop (take N == MAXVALUE). With overflow defined as UB you can say the loop executes exactly N times (because you're not allowed to write code that overflows).

So UB is both bad and a source of power :)

c.st: Why don't machine learning research agents overfit?
c.x:
And I like the bayesian interpretation too. Murphy's "Probabilistic machine learning" has an occam's razor section.

The idea is that a complex model explains many more configurations (datasets) than a simple one. So its (prior) probability distribution is lower on the data seen (to compensate for the other possibilities it might explain). So the (marginal) likelihood that the simple model is correct is higher if it fits the data well enough.

c.st: Most items of clothing have complicated international journeys
c.x:
I remember reading The Travels of a T-Shirt in the Global Economy (1) for an undergrad class about globalization - a light, quick read but one that stuck with me through college and post-graduation. Highly recommended.

The narrative follows the lifecycle of a t-shirt, from the farming of cotton in the southern US, to China where the shirts are created, back to the US for sale, and ultimately to Africa after donation.

1) https://www.amazon.com/Travels-T-Shirt-Global-Economy-Economist/dp/0471648493

c.x: I would recommend (the now outdated) The Brain that Changes Itself. All about nueroplasticiy. The brain will literally prune what you don’t use, and certain skills, such as the fine motor skills required by developing penmanship, can plausibly have wide reaching impact one way or the other.

c.st: Why I’m a sucker for pen and paper
c.x: The Brain That Changes Itself. Life changing book. One of the surprising studies there shows how kids with all kinds of learning disabilities can be radically transformed just by being given cursive handwriting exercises. Brain development and activation under handwriting is measurable, and very different from typing or even printing.

c.st: One rat brain 'talks' to another using electronic link
c.x:
Another great book with further discussion and examples on this subject, neuroplasticity, is The Brain That Changes Itself. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Brain_That_Changes_Itself

In summary from my reading of the book, current research seems to back the perspective that our brains are basically making sense of chaos: there's no standardized protocol - we automatically decode patterns from random streams of input.
